title: Network Topology Map — User Manual
summary: How to use the Topology Graph, ICMP Pinger, IP Range Scanner, Switching, and App Client Devices tabs.

sections.body:
Overview

Network Topology Map is a five-tab suite covering everything from a visual network diagram to an active subnet scanner: Topology Graph, ICMP Pinger, IP Range Scanner, Switching, and App Client Devices.

Key Features

  • Topology Graph — drag-and-drop network map with a Path Tracer, node clustering, and live status coloring.
  • ICMP Pinger — a live, single-device ping console for quick latency checks.
  • IP Range Scanner — an Angry-IP-Scanner-style subnet sweep: enter a start/end IP or pick a Netmask preset, watch live progress, and get a "Scan Statistics" summary on completion (total time, hosts scanned/alive, hosts with open ports). Hostnames resolve through three fallbacks in order: reverse DNS, then any matching Kynren agent device, then an active NetBIOS query — so hostnames still show up even without DNS records or the agent installed.
  • Switching — discover and adopt switches, then view their port maps.
  • App Client Devices — devices reported in by the Kynren Python agent (hostname, IPs, hardware info, battery).

Step-by-Step

  1. Open IP Range Scanner, enter a start/end IP (or pick a Netmask preset to auto-fill the range), and click Start.
  2. Watch the progress bar and results table fill in live; when it finishes, review the Scan Statistics popup.
  3. Click Add to Topology on any live host you want to track as a network node going forward.
  4. Switch to ICMP Pinger for a focused live check against one device.
  5. Use Switching to discover switches on the network, adopt them, and inspect their port maps.
  6. Use Topology Graph's Path Tracer to click two nodes and trace the path between them.

Tips

  • A scan is capped at 1,024 addresses at a time — split very large ranges into multiple scans.
  • The gear icon on the IP Range Scanner toolbar shows exactly which ports are probed and how hostnames are resolved.
